Ovulation happens around the middle of your cycle. The egg is ready to be fertilized.
Avoid alcohol and tobacco if you're trying to conceive.
The sperm fertilizes the egg and cell division begins. The placenta starts to form while the fertilized egg travels to the uterus.
Eat a balanced diet; many of the baby's organs will start forming very soon.
The fertilized egg implants in the uterus and starts developing as an embryo. The umbilical cord begins to form from the placenta.
If your period is late, it's a good time to take a pregnancy test and book an appointment with your doctor.
The neural tube forms, which will become the brain and spinal cord. The heart starts to form and may begin beating around now.
Start (or continue) your prenatal vitamins. Nausea may begin around this time.
The embryo takes a curved "C" shape. The first buds that will later become arms and legs appear.
Rest as much as you can and stay well hydrated; tiredness is normal in these weeks.
The brain and face grow quickly. The eyelids, the first bones and the nostrils begin to form.
If nausea is bothering you, try small, frequent meals throughout the day.
All the main organs have formed and keep maturing. From this week on, the embryo is called a fetus.
If you haven't yet, book your first prenatal appointment and ultrasound.

Stay active with gentle exercise (like walking) if your doctor says it's OK.
The head becomes rounder and the eyelids and ears keep developing.

Nausea usually starts to ease over the next few weeks — hang in there.

The first trimester ends: a good time to share the news if you'd like to.
Sex hormones start being produced. The baby can now make urine after swallowing amniotic fluid, and all the organs are formed.
You're entering the second trimester; many women notice more energy around now.
The baby can bring their hands to their mouth. Taste and smell start developing, and the skin begins to thicken.
A good time for moderate exercise or prenatal yoga.
The baby can now turn and roll over. The heart pumps a large amount of blood every day.
Watch your posture: your center of gravity is starting to shift.
The digestive system starts working. The baby can already hear some sounds.
Talk or sing to your baby: they can start hearing you now.
Vernix starts forming, a waxy substance that protects the baby's skin. Toenails begin to grow.
Keep your skin moisturized, especially your belly, which is starting to stretch.
Lanugo appears, a fine hair that covers the baby's body. The baby may wake up when you move.
If you haven't scheduled it yet, this is the usual time for the anatomy scan.
The baby's movements get stronger. The ovaries (in girls) or testicles (in boys) have formed.
Use moisturizer to ease the tight feeling on your belly.
Halfway there! Some facial features can be seen on the ultrasound and, if you want to know, the baby's sex.
Use the 20-week scan to calmly go over your baby's anatomy.
Fingers and toes are fully formed. The baby may get hiccups.
Start getting familiar with your baby's movement patterns.
The five senses are developing. The baby can already hear your voice, your heartbeat and sounds from outside.
Eat a diet rich in omega-3, which is important for brain development.
The baby may respond to your voice by moving, and spends a lot of time in REM sleep.
Keep an eye on swollen feet and ankles: it's usually normal at this stage, mention it at your appointment.

The nervous system develops quickly. The baby starts gaining some chubbiness in the cheeks.
Look after your rest; sleeping on your left side helps circulation.
The baby starts producing melanin, the skin pigment. The lungs begin producing surfactant.
Have your blood pressure checked regularly at your appointments.
The baby can now grasp. Your voice can calm them and lower their heart rate.
You're entering the third trimester: get ready for more frequent prenatal appointments.
The baby's eyes now open and close. Eyelashes start to grow.

The baby's movements are felt more and more, and more often.
Rest with your legs up now and then to ease swelling.
The lanugo gradually starts to fall off. The baby may already have some hair on their head.
Practicing breathing exercises can help you prepare for labor.
The baby now regulates their own body temperature. The bones start hardening, though the skull stays flexible.

Toenails are now visible. The skin becomes less transparent as the baby gains fat.

Slow down when you need to and make rest a priority.
The baby may start turning head-down, getting ready for birth. They keep gaining weight.
Learn to recognize the signs that labor is starting.
The skin gets pinker as the baby gains fat. The musculoskeletal system is complete.
Finish organizing everything for the hospital and at home.
The baby now takes up almost all the space inside the uterus.
From now on, prenatal appointments are usually weekly.
This is considered early term. The baby has lost almost all the lanugo and keeps gaining fat.
Go over the signs of labor with your partner or birth companion.
The liver and lungs are almost fully mature. The baby may start dropping into the pelvis.
Stay in close contact with your doctor or midwife these days.
Full term! The baby's brain keeps developing and will continue to after birth.
